904.title: Rani Sada Kaur
904.hook: a widow who led the Kanhaiya misl and backed her young son-in-law, Ranjit
904.howItsDone: Sikh histories remember Rani Sada Kaur as a leader of the Kanhaiya misl and as the ally behind the young Ranjit Singh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the misls quarreled once the danger faded; your line was danger gone, rivalry grew. Today, a woman who turned a feud into an alliance.

A betrothal between two families lately at war: that's where today begins. In one of the quarrels between the misls, Sikh histories say, Gurbakhsh Singh, son and heir of Jai Singh of the Kanhaiya misl, was killed in battle against a coalition that included the Sukerchakia misl. His widow was left with a young daughter, a grieving father-in-law and a band of riders. You met her earlier in this block. Her name was Sada Kaur.
screen: `A BETROTHAL AFTER A WAR.` → `HER HUSBAND KILLED BY THE OTHER SIDE.` → `A WIDOW WITH A DAUGHTER.`

segments.voice: The Sukerchakia chief, Maha Singh, had a son named Ranjit. Sikh histories say Sada Kaur's daughter, Mehtab Kaur, was betrothed to that boy. Her daughter was promised to the son of the chief her husband had died fighting. Some tellings credit the old chief Jai Singh with the match; in the histories, Sada Kaur is the one who made it work. A marriage turned a feud into a family. That's the first thing to see in her: she could put grief to work for peace. The second is what she did with her place. Day eight hundred ninety-one met her at the head of the Kanhaiya band, commanding its riders and managing its lands. She used that place not to settle the score, but to build something with the family on the other side of it. The third is today's line. Ranjit was young, with older, stronger chiefs all around him. Sada Kaur put her men and her judgment behind her son-in-law. When he moved, the histories say, her riders often moved with him, and her counsel went too; they give her a large part in his rise. The story doesn't stay sweet: later the two would fall out, and that comes in its own time. But at the start, when the boy had a name and not much else, a woman who had lost her husband in a feud with his family chose to stand behind him anyway.

905.title: A boy of twelve
905.hook: Maha Singh dies and his twelve-year-old son Ranjit Singh inherits the Sukerchakia misl
905.howItsDone: Sikh histories tell of Maha Singh's death and the young Ranjit Singh inheriting the Sukerchakia misl, the start of the story Sikhs remember as the rise of the Maharaja.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sada Kaur, who turned a feud into an alliance; your line was she backed him. Today, the boy she backed.

The chief of the Sukerchakia misl is out on campaign, Sikh histories say, besieging a fort, when he falls ill. He doesn't recover. Maha Singh is dead, and the band he and his father built has no grown man to lead it. What it has is his son, Ranjit: a boy, twelve years old in the usual telling, who until that day has been somebody's child. Now the riders are looking at him.
screen: `MAHA SINGH FALLS ILL ON CAMPAIGN.` → `THE CHIEF IS DEAD.` → `THE RIDERS LOOK AT RANJIT.`

segments.voice: A misl was a band of equals around a chief, and the chief's place could pass to his son. That kept the band together. It also meant the son was sometimes very young. The riders didn't get to pick a seasoned commander; they got the boy they had. So feel the weight. A boy who should be learning to ride well is suddenly the name on the banner, and every rival chief nearby notices. Some see an opening. Sikh memory already held stories of the very young carrying great weight. Guru Har Krishan became Guru as a small child, and Sikhs remember him for compassion, tending the sick in Delhi. The Guru's younger sons, the Sahibzade, stood firm at Sirhind as children. Ranjit is not a Guru and not a martyr, but the people around him had been raised on the idea that age is not the measure of a person. And a boy of twelve doesn't lead alone. Sikh histories say others helped hold the reins at first: his mother, his father's trusted men, and the family he was promised into. That help is a story for a few days from now. For today, see how the young chief begins: with grief, a band waiting for orders, and a name he hasn't grown into yet. Every later chapter starts here, with a boy standing where his father used to stand.

906.title: The Misls close
906.hook: twelve bands of equals, and the beginnings of a kingdom
906.howItsDone: Sikh histories tell the misl period as the time the Sikh bands held Punjab as confederacies of equals, before Maharaja Ranjit Singh brought them under one rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ranjit, a boy of twelve standing where his father had stood; your line was twelve, and leading. Today, this block closes.

Lay the banners out side by side. The Bhangi, strong for a time. The Ahluwalia, the leader's band. The Ramgarhia, the builders. The Kanhaiya, where Sada Kaur rose. The Sukerchakia, small beginnings. The Nakai, named for its land. The Dallewalia by the river. The Nishanwalia, carrying the flag. The Singhpuria, the nawab's band. The Karorsinghia of the Doaba. The Shaheedan, the martyrs' band. And to one side, the Phulkian houses. Tradition counts twelve.
screen: `BANNERS SIDE BY SIDE.` → `BUILDERS, FLAG-BEARERS, MARTYRS.` → `TRADITION COUNTS TWELVE.`

segments.voice: Step back and the block has a shape. It began with an idea: a misl was a band of equals with its own chief, joined to the others in the Dal Khalsa. No band owned the others, and riders could follow a chief they trusted. When something had to be decided for everyone, the bands rode to Amritsar at Vaisakhi and Diwali, sat as the Sarbat Khalsa before the Guru Granth Sahib, and agreed a gurmata that bound them all. Around the sacred pool they built bungas, rest for pilgrims and posts for defenders, and towers that still stand. That's the first movement: equals, sharing a center. The second is the strain. When the danger faded, the bands turned on each other over land and pride, and the gatherings grew harder to hold together. The third is where the block ends. Inside one band, a boy has just become chief. He is promised to the daughter of a woman who leads a misl of her own and has put her riders behind him, and he has a world of quarreling equals around him. The next part of this path follows what he did with it. The histories call him Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Sikhs remember his reign in more than one way: as a high point of Sikh rule, and as the moment the bands of equals became a kingdom. Both are part of the story.

907.title: Born at Gujranwala, 1780
907.hook: smallpox left the boy with one eye, and tradition says he laughed about it
907.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh in histories, songs and stories, and the tale of his one eye is retold as a sign that he looked on people of every faith alike.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the misls closed: bands of equals, and a kingdom starting to show; your line was equals, then a kingdom. Now a new part of the long story begins: Maharaja Ranjit Singh.

A small boy lies in a fevered room in Gujranwala, a town in the Punjab plains. The sickness is smallpox. He lives, but the histories say it leaves its marks: a scarred face, and the sight gone from one eye. Plenty of children would carry that like a weight. Tradition remembers this one differently. The boy grows up, becomes a ruler, and when people stare at the face, he laughs. The scars stay. The laughter stays too.
screen: `A FEVER IN GUJRANWALA.` → `ONE EYE GONE.` → `TRADITION SAYS HE LAUGHED.`

segments.voice: Gujranwala was the home ground of the Sukerchakia misl, the band led by the boy's father, Maha Singh. So this child was born into the misl world this path has just walked through. Nobody in that room could have known he would one day pull those bands together under one rule. Then the sickness. The sources agree on the marks it left, and they don't pretend he was handsome; some accounts describe him as short and plain, with a pitted face. What they remember is how he carried it. Now the story people love to tell. Tradition says someone once asked the Maharaja why God had given him only one eye. His answer, as the story goes: with one eye he sees everyone the same way, Hindu, Muslim and Sikh, all with a single look. It may be a story polished by years of retelling; keep it as tradition. But see what it does. It takes a loss and turns it into a joke, and the joke into a promise about how he'll rule. That promise has roots in the Guru Granth Sahib. In Sohila, the prayer Sikhs say at bedtime, Guru Nanak says that one light is within everyone, and the light in all is the light of the One. Whether or not he ever said the line about the eye, it's a very Sikh joke: the eye is less, and the seeing is more.

908.title: Leading at twelve
908.hook: young Ranjit leads the Sukerchakia misl with his mother-in-law's help
908.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Ranjit Singh's early years with Rani Sada Kaur at his side, and remember Guru Gobind Singh asking the Panj Pyare to give him amrit as a picture of a leader who receives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gujranwala: a scarred face, one eye, and a laugh; your line was one eye, clear vision. Today, the people around the boy.

A council tent. Older men with long service and longer memories sit in a ring, and at the head of it sits a boy. He has the title; his father is gone and the misl is his. What he does not have is years. He doesn't know which chief keeps his word and which one smiles and waits. He has never run a treasury. So the question in the tent isn't who's in charge. It's who's helping the one in charge.
screen: `A COUNCIL TENT.` → `A BOY AT THE HEAD OF IT.` → `WHO'S HELPING HIM?`

segments.voice: This path has met the woman at the center of this: Rani Sada Kaur, who led the Kanhaiya misl and whose daughter was married to Ranjit. Today, look at the whole circle around the boy, because the histories don't show a lone genius. They show a team. His mother held the household and the family's interests in his early years. His father's ministers and captains served. And Sada Kaur brought her own riders and her hard sense to his side; tradition credits her with steering him through the dangerous early years and standing beside him in his first big moves. Here's the turn: Ranjit didn't fight that help. He used it. Some young heirs try to prove they need nobody. Tradition remembers him learning to listen, watch and take advice until he was ready to stand on his own. That shape, a leader who receives, is an old one in Sikh memory. When Guru Gobind Singh gave amrit to the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, tradition says he then asked those five to give it to him. The Guru knelt and received. A later poet hailed him as Guru and disciple both at once. In the Sikh story, being helped is not the opposite of leading; it's part of how leading is done. The boy at the head of the tent wasn't weak because he needed people. He was a leader because he let them make him one.

909.title: Lahore, 1799
909.hook: Ranjit Singh enters Lahore, welcomed by many of its people
909.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Lahore as the city of Guru Ram Das's birth and Guru Arjan's martyrdom, and visit Gurdwara Dera Sahib there; the city later became the capital of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's kingdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Panj Pyare, and a boy carried by the people around him; your line was help makes the leader. Today, a city.

Lahore. Walls, gates, bazaars, a great fort, the domes of mosques and the roofs of temples, all crowded together. For years the city has been split among rival Sikh chiefs, and the histories say its people are tired of it. So, tradition says, some of its leading citizens, Muslim and Hindu notables among them, send word to the young Sukerchakia chief: come. Not a siege. An invitation, from inside the walls.
screen: `A CITY SPLIT AMONG RIVAL CHIEFS.` → `ITS PEOPLE SEND WORD.` → `NOT A SIEGE: AN INVITATION.`

segments.voice: First, how he came in. Tradition says Ranjit Singh rode to Lahore with his own riders and Sada Kaur's, and that friends inside opened a gate to him. There was some fighting, the histories say, but the city did not have to be broken to be taken. The rival chiefs left, and Ranjit was in. Second, what Lahore already meant to Sikhs. Sikh tradition remembers it as the birthplace of Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, and as the place where Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, was tortured and died; a gurdwara called Dera Sahib marks that spot by the river. The city held both a cradle and a grave, and now a young Sikh chief rode through its gates, not as a prisoner, but as its ruler. Third, what he did inside. The stories that come down to us show him moving carefully: keeping the city's peace, protecting its markets, showing respect to its mosques and temples alike, so that the people who had invited him would not be sorry. A welcome is easy to lose, and he seems to have known it. Not just a conquest, then, but a door that people on the other side chose to open. Lahore would be his capital for the rest of his life.

910.title: The Sarkar-e-Khalsa
910.hook: crowned Maharaja, he calls his government the Khalsa's and strikes coins in the Gurus' names
910.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh's state as the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the government of the Khalsa, and his coins, known as Nanakshahi coins, carried a verse in the names of the Gurus rather than his own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lahore, a gate opened from inside; your line was the city opened. Today, the end of a week, and a name for a kingdom.

A ruler holds the great city of the Punjab, and a new king has a question to answer: what's this called, and whose is it? The usual answer is a family name: my house, my throne, my reign, the coins carrying my face. Ranjit Singh takes the title Maharaja. And then, by the histories' account, he does something odd with it. He gives the credit away.
screen: `A NEW KING, A NEW NAME.` → `THE TITLE: MAHARAJA.` → `HE GIVES THE CREDIT AWAY.`

segments.voice: Sarkar-e-Khalsa means, roughly, the government of the Khalsa. Not of Ranjit Singh. The state, in its own name, belonged to the Khalsa, the community Guru Gobind Singh had founded, and the Maharaja was its servant, at least in the way it spoke of itself. Next, the coins. A ruler's coins are a loud announcement, passing from hand to hand across the land. Ranjit Singh's coins did not carry his own name or face. They carried a Persian verse giving the victory to Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh, a verse Sikhs had used on coins and seals before him. The money said, in effect: everything here was given by the Gurus. Then the throne. Tradition says he was reluctant to sit high, and liked to hold court sitting cross-legged on a chair or among his chiefs, and that people called him simply Sarkar, more readily than any grand title. None of this means he was shy of power; he held a great deal of it. But the way the kingdom named itself kept pointing past the king. It echoes the misl years, when bands of equals decided before the Guru, even as those bands gave way to one ruler. Some historians say it was faith, some wise politics, some both. Either way, the message was on every coin in every market.
